tagline: A pipeline haul road crosses the Yukon and the Brooks Range
intro: The Dalton Highway runs 414 miles from the Elliott Highway north of Fairbanks to Deadhorse, near the Arctic Ocean. Much of the drive is on gravel, with several steep grades. Alaska’s transportation department includes it among the state’s scenic byways and highlights a combination unique to a U.S. road: crossings of the Yukon River, Arctic Circle and Brooks Range.

Built in 1974 to supply construction of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System, the road took its name from Arctic engineer James W. Dalton. Crews completed 390 miles in five months; the pipeline followed in 1977. Public access came in stages, reaching Disaster Creek in 1981. An Alaska Supreme Court decision ordered removal of the permit requirement in 1993, and the full highway opened to the general public on December 2, 1994.

Heading north, cross the Yukon before reaching Coldfoot and Wiseman. North of Wiseman, the route passes Gates of the Arctic National Park to the west and the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to the east before reaching the pass. The highway follows the Dietrich River for 25 miles, then crosses the Continental Divide at Atigun Pass. Beyond the Brooks Range, Slope Mountain marks the gateway to the treeless coastal plain on the way to Deadhorse.
notice: At the Yukon crossing, look for the pipeline crossing the river beside the highway.

moments.title: Yukon River Bridge
moments.text: The Yukon River Bridge carries both the Dalton Highway and the pipeline, the only bridge crossing of the Yukon in Alaska. A permanent crossing was needed to complete the pipeline project. The October 1975 ribbon-cutting allowed Alyeska to use the unfinished span and avoid building an ice bridge that winter. Its driving surface is timber, supported by a steel deck and two steel box girders. In 1982, the state named it for Edward Patton, Alyeska’s former president during pipeline construction. The wooden deck has been replaced several times, including in 2007.

moments.title: Coldfoot
moments.text: Coldfoot began as a mining camp called Slate Creek. In 1902 it had two roadhouses, two stores, seven saloons and a gambling house. Its post office closed in 1912 and reopened in 1984. The town now primarily serves as a Dalton Highway truck stop. Its overnight quarters include converted pipeline construction camp accommodation. That working-road role extends to an Alaska transportation department maintenance station. The next services north are in Deadhorse, 240 miles away. A small summer visitor center brings together staff from the Bureau of Land Management, Fish and Wildlife Service and National Park Service.

moments.title: Atigun Pass
moments.text: Atigun Pass takes the Dalton Highway across the Continental Divide at mile 244. At the head of the Dietrich River, this is the only pass through the Brooks Range crossed by a road. Alaska’s transportation department identifies a turnout at the summit. The pass is maintained throughout the year, but winter brings avalanches. Farther north, the route reaches the treeless coastal plain at Slope Mountain.
